author: WoMin
title: Practising solidarity economy: Women’s collective action and community finance in Memirlosho
content:
Conversations about economic development often portray rural women as people who need support, training, or assistance. Far less attention is paid to how women organise themselves to solve problems, manage resources, and build livelihoods together. During a recent visit to the 

Memirlosho Women Cultural Village

 in Isiolo County, northern Kenya, we saw how Samburu women offer a powerful example of a community and solidarity economy in practice. The cultural village brings together four women’s groups (Narasha, Muruguti, Narupa, and Rapunye) that work as a collective to create opportunities, strengthen resilience, and improve livelihoods. Their lived experience demonstrates that solidarity economies are not solely theoretical concepts or future possibilities. They are already being built every day through cooperation, mutual support, and shared responsibility.




Collective organising as a condition for economic agency




The first foundation of Memirlosho’s economic model is collective organising. The women registered a Community Based Organisation (CBO) through which they transformed dispersed individual survival strategies into a legally recognised collective entity. This shift carries important economic and political implications as they gained greater visibility, legitimacy, and bargaining power. The umbrella structure allows the four groups to support one another while maintaining their own identities. Together, they can access external support, coordinate activities, and speak with a stronger collective voice.




More importantly, the organisation creates a sense of shared purpose. Members are no longer facing challenges alone, they have built a community that pools resources, shares risks, and works toward common goals.




Productive activities: turning livelihoods into collective assets




Memirlosho’s economic activities are rooted in skills and resources that already exist within the community. Hence, two productive activities form the backbone of the village. The first is beadwork. Women use their cultural knowledge and craftsmanship to produce traditional beadwork that can be sold for income. Working collectively allows them to purchase materials more efficiently, share information, and explore markets together.




Another important activity is goat rearing and trading. Through support from the 

Samburu Women Trust

, the groups received forty goats, with ten goats allocated to each group. Rather than viewing these animals as a one-time gift, the women transformed them into a revolving community asset.




The goats are raised and later sold, with the proceeds used to purchase new livestock. In this way, the original investment continues to generate benefits over time. Instead of being consumed, the asset grows and supports future opportunities. This approach reflects one of the central principles of solidarity economies: resources are managed not only for individual gain but for the long-term benefit of the collective.




Financial solidarity: A savings system built around people’s needs




While productive activities constitute the foundation of 

Memirlosho’s

 solidarity economy, the Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) serves as its circulatory system. The VSLA operates as a community-owned financial institution managed according to principles of mutual support rather than external profit extraction. The system has three main characteristics:




a

) Socially oriented lending:

  Women can access loans for socially important needs especially school fees, respond to emergencies, or meet household needs. Interest collected on loans is not extracted by an outside institution. Instead, it returns to the group’s common fund, benefiting all members. This way, capital serves the community’s wellbeing and social reproduction rather than simply financial accumulation.




b) Inclusive flexibility:

 The savings model is also flexible. Members contribute according to their means and circumstances, recognising that income can fluctuate throughout the year, as a pastoral community. This allows participation even during difficult periods and helps ensure that nobody is excluded because they cannot meet rigid contribution requirements. It’s a system that prioritises participation and inclusion.




c) Community control over finance:

 The VSLA enables members to maintain ownership and control over their financial resources. By keeping financial decision-making within the community, the group reduces dependence on potentially exploitative lending arrangements and strengthens collective autonomy. The system strengthens self-reliance, and finance becomes a tool for mutual support rather than a mechanism of extraction.




(Community discussions at Memirlosho Women Cultural Village hosted by Samburu Women Trust. Picture: WoMin.)




Women as builders of economic alternatives




Looking at Memirlosho through a feminist lens reveals a deeper story. Much of the work women do to sustain families and communities often goes unrecognised. Worldwide, women do 16 billion hours of unpaid care work every single day, 

according to the UN

. Caring for children, ensuring food security, paying school fees, and supporting community wellbeing are rarely considered part of “the economy,” despite being essential to everyday life. The women of Memirlosho challenge this narrow understanding of economic activity.




Their savings groups, livestock investments, and collective enterprises are not only generating income. They are helping children stay in school, manage risks, cope with emergencies, and build more secure futures. Economic activity is closely linked to care, responsibility, and community wellbeing. By organising together, women are also strengthening their voice and influence. They are managing resources, making decisions, and shaping local development on their own terms. Rather than being passive beneficiaries of development projects, they are active creators of solutions.




Accountability built on trust




A common critique of community-based financial systems is that they may lack accountability. The experience of Memirlosho demonstrates the opposite given the way accountability is managed. The organisation has developed sophisticated governance mechanisms that institutionalise trust while minimising opportunities for misuse of resources.




Firstly, the women have established bylaws that guide savings, meetings, and financial management. These are collectively agreed rules that function as a shared social contract among members. Members who miss meetings or arrive late may be fined, encouraging commitment and participation.




Secondly, an innovative colour-coded system helps members keep track of different types of contributions. Red plates are used for fines, blue plates for savings, and green plates for weekly contributions of twenty Kenyan shillings. This simple but effective system promotes transparency and accessibility, ensuring that financial transactions remain visible and understandable to all members regardless of educational background.




Thirdly, accountability is reinforced through fines for absenteeism and lateness. These mechanisms encourage participation and signal the collective value placed on commitment and responsibility.




The most striking example is the group’s triple-lock cash box system. The cash box is secured with three separate padlocks whose keys are held by different members. No individual has unilateral access to community funds. Withdrawal requires the simultaneous participation and consent of multiple individuals.




This simple system reflects an important principle: trust is strengthened when responsibility is shared. Accountability is built directly into the way resources are managed.




Building resilience in a changing climate




For pastoralist communities in Samburu, climate challenges are becoming increasingly difficult. Droughts, unpredictable rainfall, and environmental pressures create uncertainty for livelihoods and households. The institutions created by Memirlosho help members respond to these challenges. Savings provide a buffer during difficult times. Livestock function as productive assets that can be sold when necessary. Collective organisation allows members to support one another when shocks occur.




In this way, resilience is generated not only through material assets but also through collective institutions. The CBO creates social infrastructure through which members can mobilise resources, share risks, and support one another during times of uncertainty. In this sense, community solidarity becomes a form of adaptive capacity.




Challenges and limitations




While Memirlosho women cultural village demonstrates the strengths of solidarity economy practice, it also operates within broader structural constraints. Market access remains a challenge for beadwork producers, who often face difficulties accessing profitable markets without intermediaries. Livestock-based investments remain vulnerable to drought and animal disease. The success of revolving asset models may also depend on favourable environmental and economic conditions.




Furthermore, like many community-based organisations, the CBO must continuously navigate challenges related to leadership, participation, and long-term sustainability. Maintaining collective commitment and effective governance requires ongoing effort and adaptation.




Recognising these constraints does not diminish the achievements of Memirlosho. Rather, it highlights the broader structural conditions within which solidarity economy initiatives operate and the need for supportive public policies and development interventions.




“When women are together, people will see what they can do, or people will know that we are planning for something good.”

 – 

Memirlosho Women Cultural Village member




Beyond the abstract to living the alternatives




The story of Memirlosho demonstrates that solidarity economy is not an abstract idea nor a future aspiration. It is something people are already practicing through everyday acts of cooperation, mutual support, and collective stewardship and responsibility. By bringing together productive activities, community savings, shared governance, and strong accountability mechanisms, the women of Memirlosho have built an economy that places people at its centre.




Their experience shows that even small contributions, whether a goat, a bead, or a few shillings saved each week, can have a transformative impact when combined with collective organisation and shared purpose.




At a time when communities face growing economic and climate-related challenges, Memirlosho offers an inspiring example of how women are building resilient, inclusive, and caring economies from the ground up.

author: WoMin
title: Africa Can Survive Without Capitalism: Feminist School on Land and Nature Commons
content:
From 2

nd

 to 6

th

 November 2026, WoMin in collaboration with the office of 

Justice, Peace and Integration of Creation Franciscans Africa

 (JPIC – FA), hosted 35 women activists from Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania gathered in Nairobi for the 

East African Feminist School on Land and Nature Commons

.




Drawn from four distinct community struggles – pastoralist women, forest community women, women farmers and fisherfolk – the participants came together to share their experiences of resisting the dispossession of communal land and nature commons.




As part of the recommendations emerging from the 

Women’s Land Convergence

, the school sought to strengthen participants’ feminist analysis, foster cross-border solidarity, and build collective strategies towards a future beyond capitalism.




Nowhere is the drive for capitalist expansion seen more clearly than in the rush to dispossess African communities of their land and ways of life, for corporate mineral extraction, corporate food production, agrofuels, agro-industrial crops and other profit-driven ventures.




It was within this gathering that Josephine, a participant from Uganda, made a powerful declaration: “Africa can survive without capitalism.” Her words captured the political spirit of the school and the conviction shared by women whose everyday struggles challenge the destructive logic of capitalist development, especially through local solutions that have existed for centuries, such as agroforestry, artisanal fishing, intercropping, shifting cultivation, indigenous seed saving and sharing, community forest management, and peasant agroecology.




As those first and hardest hit by economic exploitation driven by profit-focused development projects, African women, continue to be at the forefront of building alternatives while remaining firmly at the centre of climate justice struggles today, even as they Face brutal oppression and violence,




Women’s Voices, Struggles and Aspirations




As the school started, the women described their challenges to the capitalist system, including constant confrontations with oil and mining corporations, local resistance to land, food and seed grabbing, and community actions against institutions of capitalist globalisation. They also shared their desire to transform the difficult struggles they wage constantly against capitalism and build a spirit of resilience and solidarity grounded in communal ownership, collective care, solidarity and respect.




Josephine, a participant from Uganda, shared with emotion and sensitivity that she hoped “to unite with other women to defend nature commons which brings peace to community. Which feeds the children and sends them to school”.




Priscilla, from Tanzania, another participant, said she hoped “

to build her knowledge around the good African culture and believe that united women together in the past in terms of communal land ownership and relationship”.




Centuries of mega-extraction have looted Africa’s land, forests, water and underground minerals, with a new wave of extraction driven by the energy transition, artificial intelligence and war. Governments continue to justify the destruction of these shared resources as development through mining projects, carbon markets and energy projects, while denying the rights of communities to say no and expropriating women’s labour without compensation.




Over five days, women told tales of exploitation and dispossession again and again, from so many different contexts: from women in farming communities whose health has been broken through endless hours of labour, toiling under harsh climate conditions; women in extractive communities condemned to the stress of perpetual insecurity and pollution; and members of communities evicted at gunpoint to make way for the next big capitalist venture on their land.




The Gendered Burdens of Extractive Capitalism




As capitalism continues to lurch from crisis to crisis, African women’s bodies continue to carry many of the burdens of the privatisation of The Commons, patriarchal modes of production, militarism and imperialism, as well as the ecological defence of the planet.




Women carry unpaid care work essential for communities to survive. The labour of care includes housework, preparing meals, caring for persons with disabilities, people who are ill or elderly family members, and birthing, raising and educating children. Across most African communities, care work is unpaid and not viewed as labour, but as ‘love’ and the ‘natural’ biological role of women.




Monica from the Benet community in Uganda reflected on this reality through her own experience: “

Being the first born of my house, I am the one who takes care of my little baby sibling. I know the problem of the child caregiving.”




Saumu, a Maasai woman from Tanzania shared that the gendered division of labour is very strong where she comes from: “

The main source of livelihood is pastoralism, it is the women who milk the cow, sheep and goats for children’s health needs. It is women who do the cooking that feeds the world, from picking of firewood in the forest under terribly conditions

.”




Nancy, a Maasai woman from Kenya described that women are central to community life: “

Because of gender roles, the women is the engine of the community. Society constructs and gives a role to women and if the women decide to stop, everything stops and if a woman dies, it is said that the house has fallen on a man.”




The participants reflections expose the centrality of women’s labour to the survival and reproduction of families and communities. Yet this labour remains largely invisible, not valued and often exploited. The contradiction becomes even more pronounced when extractive corporations enter communities and threaten the very land and resources upon which women’s reproductive and productive labour depends.




As Paulina from Tanzania described: “

When extractive profiteers come into the community, because the men want money, they will sell our community land to them without thinking about where the family will live. It is women who hold the family and community together.”




African women are among the most economically vulnerable and are perpetually in the eye of economic storms. Once nature is no longer communal, for example water sources fenced off in communities near extractive companies or plantations, it is women and girls who must walk longer distances under the sun, to fetch water from the nearest water source. When farmland is no longer available, it is women who risk sexual violence when looking for arable land to grow food.




Extractive capitalism has made it possible to privatise natural commons, land and the financialization of life. Yet these common goods wouldn’t exist if it wasn’t for the abundance, care, altruism, cooperation and communality of life that women have continued to forge and sustain within their communities. It is these relationships and practices that provide important foundations for imagining and building alternatives beyond the current development model.





































There is life Beyond Capitalism




At the end of the school, women shared alternatives they are already building against the destructive, profit-driven capitalist development model. Women are at the forefront of seed conservation, sharing and distributing seeds, especially during climate disasters, and keeping them alive through practice and exchange. This living tradition challenges capitalist seed banks that rely on laboratory storage.




Across East Africa, women are saying YES to collective ownership and governance of land and natural resources, free, prior, informed and continuous consent, women’s participation in community decision-making and development that sustains life and restores the environment.




In Tanzania, pastoralist and hunter-gatherer communities are working together to protect common grazing fields and ancestral lands.







“

For us, pastoralist communities, we work together with hunters and gatherers. We live in the forest. We come together in grazing fields. We think about our ancestors, how they left this Earth, what they taught us… This is something that we can do to continue to take care of our land, our culture. We started this 35 years ago.” –

 

Paulina, Tanzania







In Kenya, women are identifying collective resources and ancestral sites, protecting sacred places and ensuring Indigenous knowledge is passed on to younger generations.  







“

We are protecting our land, our resources, so that nobody comes and destroys our sacred places, nobody comes and destroys where animals go to get water. Most of the knowledge is disappearing. We are identifying our collective resources, our ancestral sites, and we will have this knowledge transferred from our generation to another.” –

 

Alice, Kenya







Women in coastal communities of Kenya and Tanzania are also practising seaweed farming as an alternative source of income and for medicine, soap, food etc. These practices sustain livelihoods and reflect feminist economies of care that value health, time, wellbeing and sustenance.  As Fridiana from Tanzania shared: 

“When we look at the ocean, there isn’t just fish, there is also seaweed that we depend on. We get medicine, we get porridge for our children. When they come and destroy these things, we don’t just lose the fish.”




Through these efforts, African women continue to build alternatives, while demanding and fighting for land rights and defending the commons in ways that strengthen collective resilience. The task therefore is to recognise, strengthen and build upon the knowledge, practices and relationships women have sustained for centuries, despite capitalism.

author: WoMin
title: Women Unite to Defend the Congo Basin Against Extractivism – A Call for Climate Justice at COP31
content:
As world leaders gather in Antalya, Türkiye, for the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), taking place from 9–20 November 2026, women from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the Republic of Congo and Cameroon are raising an urgent message: there can be no climate justice without defending the Congo Basin, protecting community territories and recognising the leadership of women on the frontlines of environmental struggles.




The Congo Basin is one of the world’s most important ecological treasures, acting as the “

second lungs

 of the Earth”, after the Amazon, which is being decimated. Spanning over four million square kilometres across six countries, its forests, rivers and peatlands play a vital role in regulating the global climate, protecting biodiversity and sustaining millions of people. For Indigenous Peoples and local communities, the forest is not simply a natural resource; it is their home, heritage, identity and source of life.




Yet this vital ecosystem faces growing threats from mining, logging, oil and gas extraction, deforestation and expanding infrastructure. Across the Congo Basin, rising demand for minerals is increasing pressure on forests and community territories.




Recent investigations have 

documented

 mining concessions overlapping with community forests in the DRC, gold-mining-related 

forest destruction and water pollution

 in the Republic of Congo, and 

concerns over the impacts

 of the Lobé-Kribi iron-ore project on forests and livelihoods in Cameroon.




This exposes a growing contradiction: while governments promote renewable energy as a solution to the climate crisis, the extraction of minerals needed for the energy transition can create new threats to forests, water resources and the communities that depend on them.




For women in the Congo Basin, this is not an abstract debate. It means polluted rivers, disappearing food sources, loss of agricultural land and declining access to forests.




Women on the frontlines expose the cost of extractivism




To strengthen collective resistance, women and community organisations from the DRC, the Republic of Congo and Cameroon came together for a 

cross-border solidarity exchange

 to share stories of resistance, expose the impacts of extractivism and develop strategies to defend the Congo Basin.




Over three days, organisations including 

Centre d’Encadrement pour la Promotion de la Femme et la jeune fille

 (CEPF), 

Dynamique des femmes pour le développement

 (DYFED), 

Green Development Advocates

 (GDA), and the Association pour le Respect des Droit des population autochtones et du développement rural et du Droit de l’homme (ARPA2DH) 

shared their experiences and struggles. Testimonies from women in Lessoukou, Mayoko, Mangi, Bongonde and Bandzonko revealed the devastating impacts of mining and forest exploitation.




In Lessoukou, 17 of the community’s 24 villages are reportedly occupied by mining companies, threatening access to ancestral lands and traditional livelihoods. Élisé Matsanga, an Indigenous woman from Lessoukou, shared:







“

Agriculture once enabled us to feed our families and send our children to school. Today, because of corporate activities and the loss of access to our lands, we can no longer farm as we used to. We have lost our livelihoods

.”







In Mangi, Tshopo Province, Nyota described how communities are excluded from decisions affecting their territories while rivers become increasingly polluted.







“

We are forced to walk up to three kilometres to find safe drinking water, and sometimes even our children have no choice but to drink polluted water. Our lands, forests and rivers are our sources of livelihood, yet we watch helplessly as they are destroyed

.”







In Bandzonko, Republic of Congo, Odile, the village chief, 

described how mining pollution

 has forced women to walk up to 15 kilometres in search of water, exposing families to serious health risks. In Bongonde, Équateur Province, Annie Mboyo, a community woman, 

highlighted the disappearance

 of mushrooms, caterpillars, wild fruits and fish, resources that have traditionally sustained community food systems. Meanwhile, in Mayoko, Oko Jeanine, another community woman, denounced the lack of consultation and the destruction of agricultural fields by mining companies.







“

These lands belong to us. They are our heritage, our livelihoods and our identity. How can companies demand that we obtain permits to cultivate our own land while they extract minerals without consulting us?

”







These testimonies reveal that extractivism is not only rapidly destroying forests and ecosystems; it is also undermining women’s rights, food sovereignty, safety and dignity. Indigenous women face additional discrimination, land dispossession and heightened exposure to gender-based violence.




Beyond climate promises: communities demand accountability




As COP31 comes to a close, African women’s experiences bring urgency to discussions on the transition to clean energy and forest protection.




One prominent initiative on the table in this round of negotiations is the 

proposed 35-by-35 electrification pledge

, which aims to increase electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035. While this ambition supports the transition to cleaner energy, it also raises questions about growing mineral demand and the environmental and social costs of extraction.




COP31’s 

focus on stewarding forests, oceans and biodiversity

 is equally important for the Congo Basin. Protecting these ecosystems must mean more than recognising their role in regulating the global climate; it must also mean defending the rights, livelihoods and territories of the Indigenous Peoples and local communities who depend on them.




There can be no green transition that sacrifices the territories, livelihoods and rights of the people who protect our forests. Women on the frontlines are calling for a just transition that guarantees Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), upholds the Right to Say NO, protects community forests and ensures meaningful participation in decisions affecting their territories.




The question for COP31 is not simply how quickly the world can transition to cleaner energy, but whose lands, resources and livelihoods will pay the price?




The women of the Congo Basin remind world leaders that there can be no climate justice without protecting forests, respecting community rights and recognising women’s leadership.










(WoMin staff attending COP31 in Turkey. Picture: WoMin)










From solidarity to collective action




Beyond sharing experiences, participants at the cross-border exchange developed a common action plan to strengthen women’s leadership and community resistance. Priorities included mapping iron ore activities and impacts, strengthening knowledge of legal protections, promoting the Right to Say NO and FPIC, improving risk and safety strategies, and building advocacy.




One immediate commitment was to launch a collective advocacy action demanding access to safe drinking water for communities affected by extractive activities. These commitments demonstrate that women are not simply victims of environmental destruction. They are organisers, knowledge holders, defenders of territories and leaders of alternatives that place life, collective care and ecological sustainability at the centre.




Defending the Congo Basin is defending life




The cross-border exchange reaffirmed that protecting the Congo Basin cannot be separated from protecting the rights of the women, Indigenous Peoples and communities who have safeguarded these territories for generations.




As world leaders deliberate over climate solutions at COP31, the voices of women from the Congo Basin must not remain on the margins of global climate discussions. United across borders, these women and communities show that collective power and solidarity can challenge extractivism and defend the forests, territories, and livelihoods of present and future generations. Defending the Congo Basin 

is

 defending life, dignity and the future of our planet.

author: WoMin
title: From Mombasa to Yaoundé, the vision and the demand is for reparative justice
content:
Through WoMin’s work alongside African women organising against extractivism, against the drivers of the climate crisis and its impacts, the destruction of the commons through false solutions, unjust energy transitions (and generally a world order that serves a minority over the global majority), we have been asking: what is the full range of impacts and costs in the face of environmental and climate impacts? Who and whose work absorbs these impacts and costs? And what would repair mean from the perspective of women, their communities and the ecosystems they care for and are cared for at the frontline of the climate crisis, where centuries of continued systems of accumulation by dispossession and destruction meet?




Our experience shows us that reparations cannot simply be another form of compensation. They must confront the very systems producing the harm – extractivism, odious and illegitimate debt, colonial legacies, patriarchy, racism, and corporate power promoting more false solutions whose aim is not climate justice but profit. Reparations must indeed offer us all a real chance to build Pan African feminist futures that centre care, including the restoration of the commons, and the conditions that make life possible.




Connecting the “c-words” – colonialism to climate reparations




The recent 

African Symposium on Climate Reparations

 in Mombasa, Kenya, started on
